The endings -ais, -ait, -aient all sound like an open “e”, as in “bed”: je parlais, il parlait, ils parlaient = “par-LEH”. As in the present, many forms sound the same.
Only nous and vous have different endings: nous parlions = “par-LYÕ”, vous parliez = “par-LYAY”. You hear a short “y”.
You can hear the difference between passé composé and imparfait: “j’ai parlé” (closed e, as in “day”) versus “je parlais” (open e, as in “bed”). Practise them as a pair.
The imparfait of être: j’étais = “zhay-TEH”, il était = “eel ay-TEH”, nous étions = “noo-zay-TYÕ”.
Noël = “no-EL”, two syllables. The diaeresis (¨) on ë shows the vowels are pronounced separately.
1. The imparfait: how to form it
The imparfait is the second French past tense. It corresponds to English “used to…”, “was …ing” and descriptive “was / had”: “I used to live, I was eating, it was nice”.
The rule is very simple, with almost no exceptions: take the NOUS form of the present, drop -ons and add the endings.
More examples: nous allons → j’allais, nous avons → j’avais, nous prenons → je prenais, nous buvons → je buvais, nous venons → je venais.
The only exception: ÊTRE. Its stem is “ét-”: j’étais, tu étais, il était, nous étions, vous étiez, ils étaient.
The imparfait has three main jobs:
description in the past (setting, weather, people)
Il faisait beau. La maison était grande.
The weather was nice. The house was big.
Chaque été, nous allions à la mer.
I was six. I was happy.

Words that call for the imparfait: d’habitude (usually), chaque jour / chaque été (every day / summer), tous les dimanches, toujours, souvent, autrefois (in the old days), quand j’étais petit(e) (when I was little).
3. Imparfait or passé composé? The first rule
The difference is close to English “I used to eat / I was eating” versus “I ate”:
Je mangeais (I used to eat / was eating): habit, duration, setting
J’ai mangé (I ate): finished action, once
Chaque Noël, ma grand-mère faisait du cozonac.
Ce Noël, ma grand-mère a fait du cozonac.
Il a neigé hier soir. (an event)

Tip: if in English you could say “used to” or “was …ing” (or it’s a description: it was, he had), use the imparfait. If it’s a single completed event (“I went, I saw”), use the passé composé. That works in 90% of cases!
In chapter 14 you’ll combine them in the same story: “Il pleuvait (setting) quand je suis arrivée (event).”
4. The pronominal verb SE SOUVENIR DE
“Se souvenir de” (to remember) is conjugated like “venir” (chapter 7), with a reflexive pronoun:
Don’t forget “de”: “Je me souviens DE toi” (I remember you). A simpler synonym: “se rappeler” + direct object: “Je me rappelle mon enfance”.
In the south of France, Christmas has special traditions, which you can describe perfectly with the imparfait:
The dinner on the evening of 24 December, “le gros souper”, with fish and vegetables.
Thirteen desserts, for Jesus and the twelve apostles: nuts, figs, dates, white and black nougat, “pompe à l’huile”…
Small clay figurines in the crib: the shepherd, the baker, the fisherman, all the villagers.
Trap: “le réveillon” isn’t “the waking up”, even though it comes from “se réveiller”. It’s the long Christmas Eve dinner where you “stay awake” past midnight.

On 24 December, at three in the afternoon, the kitchen of the old house was a mess.
There was flour everywhere: on the table, on the floor, and even in Julien’s hair.
Julien was reading his grandmother’s recipe book aloud. “A little flour, a little sugar… But how much is a little?”
Ioana was laughing. “Your grandmother never measured anything. Nor did mine! She used to say: ‘The hands know.’”
They started with the easy things. The walnuts, figs, almonds and raisins are the “four beggars”. They just had to put them in little bowls.
Then the oranges, tangerines, dates and winter melon. Nine desserts already!
But the last four were harder. The white nougat and the black nougat they bought at the pastry shop by the port. “Grandma didn’t make them either,” said Julien.
That left the pompe à l’huile and the oreillettes, little fritters.
The pompe à l’huile came out of the oven completely flat and a bit burnt. Julien pulled a face.
“When Grandma made it, it was big and golden…”
So Ioana took the dough for the oreillettes. She worked fast, without looking at the book. She did exactly what her grandmother did in Iași when she made gogoși.
Ten minutes later there was a mountain of golden fritters on the table, with icing sugar.
Julien tasted one and closed his eyes. “That’s exactly the taste of my childhood. How did you do it?”
Ioana smiled. “I didn’t read the book. The hands know.”
In the evening they ate the thirteen desserts in front of the fireplace. The pompe à l’huile was burnt, but nobody said so.
Outside the sea was calm and the stars were shining. It was a perfect Christmas.
